desc:
Rotate the array nums to the right by k steps and return the rotated array. One step moves the last element to the front and shifts everything else one place to the right.

k can be far larger than the length of the array. Try to do the rotation with O(1) extra space besides the returned array (reversals make this possible).

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], k = 3
result = [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]
hints: Rotating by n steps gives back the same array. So only k mod n matters.
Look at the target: the last k elements move to the front, in their original order, followed by the first n - k elements.
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n - k elements.
editorial: Reduce k to k mod n first, since a full turn changes nothing. After that, the rotated array is the last k elements followed by the first n - k elements.

Slicing builds this directly in O(n) extra space. To avoid the extra space, use three reversals: reversing the whole array puts the last k elements at the front but backwards, and the first n - k elements at the back but backwards. Reversing each of the two blocks again restores their order. Every element is swapped a constant number of times, so the time is O(n).
Simulating one step at a time costs O(n * k), which is far too slow once k reaches the billions.
solution:
def rotateArray(nums, k):
    a = list(nums)
    n = len(a)
    k %= n

    def rev(i, j):
        while i < j:
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
            i += 1
            j -= 1

    rev(0, n - 1)
    rev(0, k - 1)
    rev(k, n - 1)
    return a
